Imagine a kingdom that once ruled the whole archipelago.
A kingdom that drove back the strongest army in the world.
Yet the same kingdom fell, not to an enemy from outside, but to a fight inside its own house.
This is the story of Majapahit, from the fire that gave it birth, to the wound that brought it down.
Chapter one. Fire over Singhasari.
The year is 1292. Singhasari is at the height of its power, under King Kertanegara.
He refused Kublai Khan, ruler of the Mongols, and even humiliated his envoy.
But in Kediri, a ruler nursed an old grudge. His name was Jayakatwang.
When Singhasari let its guard down, Jayakatwang struck. Kertanegara was killed, and the palace burned.
In the chaos, the king's son-in-law, Raden Wijaya, escaped with his followers.
He fled to Madura, and asked Arya Wiraraja for protection.
With Arya Wiraraja's help, Raden Wijaya pretended to surrender to Jayakatwang.
Jayakatwang believed him, and gave him the forest of Tarik.
But it was all an act.
There, Raden Wijaya quietly built a base. His followers cut down trees, and ate the fruit of the maja, which tasted bitter.
That, as the story goes, is how Majapahit got its name.
Meanwhile, across the sea, Kublai Khan had not forgotten the insult to his envoy.
According to Chinese records, he sent some twenty to thirty thousand troops, with hundreds of ships, to punish Kertanegara.
But the moment they landed on Java, they heard confusing news. Kertanegara was already dead, and Jayakatwang was in power.
The Mongol commanders lost their bearings. Who was the real enemy?
That was when Raden Wijaya saw a golden opportunity.
He declared his loyalty to Kublai Khan, and offered to work together.
Your enemy is in Kediri. Let's attack together!
In April 1293, the allied army stormed Daha, the capital of Kediri.
The battle lasted from morning until afternoon. Kediri fell, and Jayakatwang surrendered.
The Mongol commanders thought their mission was done.
But this was the turning point.
Raden Wijaya asked to go home to prepare tribute, and two princesses as gifts for the Emperor.
He asked for unarmed escorts, because, he said, the princesses feared weapons.
On the road, that party was ambushed. Then the main Mongol camp was suddenly attacked.
More than three thousand Mongols were killed, and the rest fled to their ships.
In late May 1293, the strongest army in the world sailed home to China.
Months later, around November 1293, Raden Wijaya was crowned the first king of Majapahit, as Kertarajasa Jayawardhana.
This war was not won by the biggest army, but by the smartest strategy.
Chapter two. A wedding that became a tragedy.
Sixty-four years later, Majapahit is at its peak, under King Hayam Wuruk and Prime Minister Gajah Mada.
Gajah Mada once swore the Palapa Oath. He would not enjoy palapa until the archipelago was united under Majapahit.
One kingdom still had not bowed. Sunda.
In 1357, Hayam Wuruk fell in love with Dyah Pitaloka, the princess of Sunda, and proposed.
King Linggabuana agreed. He sailed to Majapahit with his family and a small party, fewer than a hundred people.
They did not bring an army, because they came for a wedding.
They camped at Bubat Field near the capital, waiting for the wedding day.
But Gajah Mada had other plans.
He rejected an equal marriage. Dyah Pitaloka must be handed over as an offering, a sign that Sunda had submitted.
King Linggabuana was furious. The wedding was cancelled, and he chose to go home with his head held high.
But Majapahit troops had surrounded Bubat.
The Sundanese were hopelessly outnumbered, dozens against thousands.
Yet they chose to fight to the end. King Linggabuana fell.
According to tradition, Dyah Pitaloka took her own life to protect her honor.
Hayam Wuruk is said to have grieved, and regretted it.
Gajah Mada lost the court's trust, and was retired to Madakaripura.
Majapahit and Sunda stayed estranged for centuries.
Historians still debate the details. The story appears in the Kidung Sunda, the Carita Parahyangan and the Pararaton, but not in the Nagarakretagama.
One political ambition turned a celebration of love into a scar on history.
Chapter three. A war inside the house.
In 1389, Hayam Wuruk died, and Majapahit split in two.
In the Western Court ruled Wikramawardhana, the king's nephew and son-in-law.
In the East ruled Bhre Wirabhumi, Hayam Wuruk's son by a concubine, according to the Pararaton.
Both felt they had the greater right. The quarrel grew, until Bhre Wirabhumi sought support from the Emperor of China.
In 1404, the Paregreg War erupted.
Regreg, in Old Javanese, means moving in halts and jerks, and this war indeed lurched back and forth.
First the west won, then the east.
Two years of war drained the royal treasury, and left the soldiers exhausted.
In 1406, the western army, led by Bhre Tumapel, broke into the Eastern Court.
Bhre Wirabhumi fled by boat at night, but was hunted down and killed by Raden Gajah.
The Western Court won. But it was a hollow victory.
In the chaos, about one hundred and seventy Ming envoys visiting the Eastern Court were killed too.
Emperor Yongle demanded sixty thousand taels of gold. By 1408, only ten thousand had been paid, and the rest was forgiven.
Vassal lands began to stop paying tribute, and broke away one by one.
The Paregreg War is thought to be one cause of Majapahit's decline. The kingdom finally came to an end around the early sixteenth century.
From the fire of Singhasari to a civil war, Majapahit left two lessons.
A clever strategy can defeat the biggest army.
But no matter how strong a kingdom is, its deadliest enemy often comes from within.
Majapahit. 1293 to 1527.
